li.a: The Encyclopedia of Saskatchewan: Cypress Hills Massacre
The Canadian Encyclopedia: Cypress Hills Massacre, by Philip Goldring
Parks Canada: History of Fort Walsh National Historic Site
The Canadian Encyclopedia: North-West Mounted Police, by Edward Butts
Dictionary of Canadian Biography: Walsh, James Morrow

content.p: On the morning of 1 June 1873, in a valley in the Cypress Hills of what is now southwestern Saskatchewan, a group of drunken traders, wolf hunters and Métis freighters fired into an Assiniboine camp from the cover of a coulee. The Canadian Encyclopedia says at least 20 men, women and children died beside Battle Creek. The Canadian Encyclopedia says the Assiniboine killed only one wolfer, a French-Canadian named Ed Legrace. Nobody was convicted. The killings are remembered mainly for what they were said to have done to Canadian policy, and Parks Canada also records that the Nakoda people who survived suffered further cruelty after the shooting stopped.
content.h2: A hard winter and a crowded valley
content.p: The Encyclopedia of Saskatchewan traces the violence to the fierce competition for buffalo robes, furs and whisky in the area. The hills lay far from the Hudson's Bay Company's Red and Saskatchewan river posts, yet traders from Fort Benton, Montana, had pushed in by 1870 with large amounts of illegal whisky. Philip Goldring, writing for the Canadian Encyclopedia, says their presence underlined how weak Canadian authority was west of Winnipeg.

The winter of 1872-73 was a hard one for the Assiniboine, led by Chief Little Soldier (Manitupotis), because food on the prairies was becoming scarce. At the end of May 1873 they were camped beside the north fork of the Milk River, where another small band under Chief Inihan Kinyen joined them. Together the two camps held about 300 people, fifty of them soldier-warriors, according to the Encyclopedia of Saskatchewan. Goldring describes the camp as 50 lodges.

Within sight of the camp stood two small log posts run by Montana traders. Abel Farwell's was on the west bank of the creek, and Moses Solomon's stood across it to the northeast. Hundreds of Métis who followed the shrinking bison herds also wintered in the hills. By late May relations were bitter. The Assiniboine believed Solomon was cheating them and had shot into his post, and the Saskatchewan encyclopedia says they threatened to clear out the traders and kill them if they resisted.

The spark came from somewhere else. About two weeks earlier, a party of about a dozen wolfers had been returning to Fort Benton with their season's take when forty of their horses were stolen. The herd had not been closely guarded because they did not expect a raid so close to the town. Thomas Hardwick, whom the Saskatchewan encyclopedia calls the Green River Renegade, and his men gave up the chase and went to Fort Benton. Goldring says the horses were probably taken by Cree, and that the wolfers tracked them north into Canada, lost the trail and arrived at Farwell's place in a foul mood.

The wolfers arrived on the last day of May. They searched for their animals, but Farwell told them that Little Soldier's people were poor and had very few horses. That evening they drank with Métis freighters who had recently arrived, and they began again early the next morning, with Solomon joining in.

Around noon, according to the Encyclopedia of Saskatchewan, a horse belonging to a trader named George Hammond went missing. He shouted that the Assiniboine had taken it, and asked the wolfers to help him seize Assiniboine horses in retaliation. The men took up their rifles and went toward the camp with some Métis freighters, all of them drunk. Alexis Labombarde found that the horse had simply wandered off and shouted so to the men, but by then, the encyclopedia says, few were willing to listen.

The sequence from there is uncertain, and both encyclopedias say so. Goldring writes that it can only be pieced together from many contradictory witness statements. Farwell later said he tried to talk the men out of violence and, when that failed, waded across to the Assiniboine camp. He claimed he struck a deal with a headman to hold two Assiniboine horses until the missing animal was found, although, the Saskatchewan encyclopedia notes, he knew little or no Assiniboine. A Métis man ran to the camp to warn the people, and they began to flee. Hammond tried to take two horses and was stopped by an armed warrior called Bighead. He went back to the wolfers and freighters, who by then lined the edge of a coulee overlooking the exposed camp on two sides. Farwell told the Assiniboine to scatter.

Then someone, possibly Hammond according to the Saskatchewan encyclopedia, fired a shot, and indiscriminate fire followed. Goldring says accounts differ about who fired first, and that some Assiniboine even challenged the armed traders and wolfers to fight. Shooting from the shelter of the coulee with Winchester and Henry repeating rifles, the attackers overwhelmed a camp that had few modern weapons. People ran for timber about fifty metres to the east, hid in the bushes beside the coulee or crossed the river, and many were shot as they fled, Inihan Kinyen among them. The Assiniboine muskets and arrows killed one wolfer, Legrace, who the Canadian Encyclopedia says still lies in a rough wooden coffin beneath where Solomon's post stood.

Goldring writes that the Assiniboine dead were not buried and that bones lay on the site for years. The survivors reached safety with some Métis a few kilometres away. The Montana traders packed up and went south, escorted by the wolfers.

The sources do not agree on the count. The Encyclopedia of Saskatchewan says approximately twenty Assiniboine died. The Canadian Encyclopedia says at least 20. Its separate entry on the North-West Mounted Police says more than 30 were killed. Parks Canada says only that many Nakoda people were killed. These are historians' and officials' estimates drawn from contradictory testimony, and none of the pages fixes an exact number.

The news travelled slowly. Farwell reported it to authorities in Montana, who passed it to Washington, while Métis brought word to Winnipeg too. Goldring says the two reports arrived in Ottawa around the close of August 1873.

Ottawa then spent three years trying to see the killers answer in court. Goldring says that in July 1875 officers of the newly formed North West Mounted Police went to Montana without managing to extradite seven men. Another three, captured in Canada, were tried in Winnipeg and acquitted in June 1876. Goldring explains that the fight had been chaotic, and no sworn witness would name any one prisoner as guilty. All charges were dropped in 1882. He adds that the United States government cooperated, but that public opinion in Montana favoured the accused, while in Winnipeg it was divided.

Because no court found anyone guilty, nobody involved can be named as a convicted killer. The sources describe the attackers as groups of traders, wolfers and freighters, and the individuals named above appear in witness accounts and historians' reconstructions, not in a verdict.
content.h2: A police force already on the way
content.p: The massacre is often credited with creating the North West Mounted Police, but the pages are careful on this. The Canadian Encyclopedia's police entry says Parliament passed the act for a Mounted Police Force for the North-West Territories on 23 May 1873, before the killings. Goldring agrees that the legislation came first. Cabinet discussed the whisky trade in early August, and on 28 August the Ottawa Citizen announced the force would be organized at once. The next day brought the first eastern Canadian press report on the massacre. Goldring says the eastern press paid little attention, absorbed in the fall of Sir John A. Macdonald's scandal-plagued government on 5 November, by which time the first 150 recruits were already training in Manitoba.

Parks Canada says the news confirmed the government's fear of a lawless West and led to the Great March West. About 300 recruits set out from Fort Dufferin on 8 July 1874. The police entry gives the distance as 1,300 kilometres, while Parks Canada says some fifteen hundred. The Encyclopedia of Saskatchewan says the massacre is generally credited with prompting the decision to create the force.
Goldring adds that officials hoped the investigation would show First Nations that the justice system was impartial, and that at first it probably did.
content.h2: Fort Walsh and the site today
content.p: In 1875 Inspector James Morrow Walsh took B Division to the Cypress Hills and established Fort Walsh, which the Dictionary of Canadian Biography calls the most important police establishment for the next seven years. Its importance grew after Sitting Bull and several thousand Sioux took refuge in Canada following the Little Bighorn in 1876. Fort Walsh was police headquarters from 1878 until 1882, then was abandoned the following year.

The ground where the Assiniboine were attacked is now the Cypress Hills Massacre National Historic Site. Parks Canada says reconstructions of Farwell's and Solomon's trading posts were built there in 1967 as a Centennial project.
